source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 18 (PDF 83-114, printed 83-114); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 18 (Inheritance), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 A plant that produces all offspring with the same trait upon self-fertilization is called:
blocks.explanation: A plant that is true-breeding (pure-breeding) for a trait produces all offspring with the same trait on self-fertilization (18.1).

book_ref.quote: produces all the offspring with the same trait upon self-fertilization

blocks.prompt: 2 In his first monohybrid crosses, Mendel observed the inheritance of:
blocks.explanation: Mendel's first monohybrid crosses followed seed shape: round × wrinkled gave all round F1 seeds (18.1).

book_ref.quote: In the first monohybrid crosses, he observed the inheritance of

blocks.prompt: 3 The alternative trait that was not expressed in the F1 plants was called by Mendel:
blocks.explanation: The trait expressed in F1 (round) was dominant; the alternative trait not expressed in F1 (wrinkled) was recessive (18.1).

book_ref.quote: the alternative trait that was not expressed in the F1 plants

blocks.prompt: 4 Mendel's results suggested that the 3:1 ratio of the F2 generation was really a disguised:
blocks.explanation: The F2 3:1 ratio was a disguised 1:2:1: 1/4 pure-breeding dominant, 2/4 not pure-breeding dominant, 1/4 pure-breeding recessive (18.1).

book_ref.quote: the 3:1 ratio in F2 generation was really a disguised 1:2:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 5 In Mendel's F2 generation, the fraction that was dominant but NOT pure-breeding was:
blocks.explanation: In F2, 1/4 were pure-breeding dominant, 2/4 were not pure-breeding dominant and 1/4 were pure-breeding recessive (18.1).

book_ref.quote: 2/4 were not pure-breeding dominant

blocks.prompt: 6 The chromosomal theory of inheritance was proposed in 1902 by:
blocks.explanation: In 1902 the American scientist Walter Sutton proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance (18.1).

book_ref.quote: In 1902, American scientist Walter Sutton proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance

blocks.prompt: 7 The German geneticist who rediscovered Mendel's work in 1900 and suggested the role of chromosomes in heredity was:
blocks.explanation: In 1900 Karl Correns rediscovered Mendel's work and suggested the role of chromosomes in heredity (18.1).

book_ref.quote: In 1900, German geneticist Karl Correns, rediscovered

blocks.prompt: 8 According to the chromosomal theory, Mendel's laws are explained by the behaviour of chromosomes during:
blocks.explanation: The theory states that genes are at specific locations on chromosomes and that the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis explains Mendel's laws (18.1).

book_ref.quote: The behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis explains

blocks.prompt: 9 Mendel concluded that the trait which 'disappeared' in the F1 hybrids:

options.text: was permanently lost from the plants
was changed into the dominant trait
was disguised in the F1 seeds and reappeared in 1/4 of F2 seeds

blocks.explanation: The trait not expressed in F1 reappeared in 1/4 of F2 seeds, so it must have been disguised in the F1 seeds (18.1).

book_ref.quote: must therefore be disguised in the F1 seeds

blocks.prompt: 10 Mendel's special 'factors' that control the characters of organisms are now called:
blocks.explanation: Mendel said characters are controlled by special 'factors', which are now called genes (18.1).

book_ref.quote: which are now called genes

blocks.prompt: 11 The alternative forms of a gene, leading to alternative traits, are called:
blocks.explanation: All copies of a gene may not be identical; its alternative forms are called alleles (18.1).

book_ref.quote: The alternative forms of a gene, leading to alternative traits, are called alleles

blocks.prompt: 12 The particular location of a gene on a chromosome is called its:
blocks.explanation: The particular location of a gene on a chromosome is the gene's locus (18.1).

book_ref.quote: The particular location of a gene on a chromosome is called the gene

blocks.prompt: 13 An offspring formed by the fusion of two gametes carrying the same allele is:
blocks.explanation: When two gametes with the same alleles fuse, the offspring is homozygous; with different alleles it is heterozygous (18.1).

book_ref.quote: Such offspring is called homozygous for that gene pair or trait

blocks.prompt: 14 Which statement correctly relates genotype and phenotype?

options.text: Phenotype is the blueprint; genotype is the visible outcome
Both mean the combination of alleles
Genotype is only the dominant allele
Genotype is the blueprint; phenotype is the visible outcome

blocks.explanation: The combination of alleles is the genotype (the blueprint); the observable trait is the phenotype (the visible outcome) (18.1).

book_ref.quote: the genotype is the blueprint, and the phenotype is the visible outcome

blocks.prompt: 15 A gene is now defined as a sequence of nucleotides, as part of DNA, which codes for the formation of a:
blocks.explanation: A gene is 'a sequence of nucleotides as part of DNA, which codes for the formation of a polypeptide' (18.1).

book_ref.quote: which codes for the formation of a polypeptide

blocks.prompt: 16 The principle that each gamete receives just one allele of a gene, selected randomly, is the:
blocks.explanation: When gametes form, each receives one allele selected randomly; this is the law of segregation (18.1).

book_ref.quote: each gamete receives just one gene copy (allele), which is selected randomly

blocks.prompt: 17 In a testcross, an individual with a dominant phenotype is crossed with:
blocks.explanation: A testcross determines whether a dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous by crossing it with a recessive phenotype (18.1).

book_ref.quote: It involves crossing the dominant phenotype with a recessive phenotype

blocks.prompt: 18 A round-seeded plant crossed with a wrinkled-seeded plant (rr) gives round and wrinkled offspring in a 1:1 ratio. The round parent was:
blocks.explanation: In a testcross an Rr plant gives round and wrinkled offspring 1:1, while an RR plant gives all round (Rr) offspring (18.1).

book_ref.quote: If it is Rr, the offspring will be round and wrinkled in a 1:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 19 The F1 plants of the cross RRYY × rryy are called dihybrids because they:

options.text: carry two pairs of sex chromosomes

blocks.explanation: All F1 seeds (RrYy) were round and yellow and heterozygous for both genes, so they are called dihybrids (18.2).

book_ref.quote: These F1 plants are called dihybrids, as they are heterozygous for both genes

blocks.prompt: 20 How many kinds of gametes does an F1 dihybrid plant (RrYy) produce?
blocks.explanation: An RrYy plant forms four gamete combinations: RY, Ry, rY and ry (18.2).

book_ref.quote: During gamete formation, four combinations are produced: RY, Ry, rY, ry

blocks.prompt: 21 When the gametes of two F1 dihybrids combine, the number of combinations formed in F2 is:
blocks.explanation: 4 male × 4 female gametes give 16 combinations in F2, showing four phenotypes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio (18.2).

book_ref.quote: 16 combinations are formed in the F2 generation

blocks.prompt: 22 In Mendel's dihybrid F2 (9:3:3:1), the phenotype in the smallest class '1' is:
blocks.explanation: The F2 ratio is 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green (18.2).

book_ref.quote: This results in four phenotypes in F2 in a 9:3:3:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 23 In the F2 of Mendel's dihybrid cross, round versus wrinkled seeds considered alone show the ratio:
blocks.explanation: Independent assortment does not affect segregation of each allele pair, so round:wrinkled is 3:1 and yellow:green is also 3:1 (18.2).

book_ref.quote: Thus, round vs wrinkled seeds show a 3:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 24 The modern re-statement of Mendel's law of independent assortment is that genes assort independently during meiosis when they are:

options.text: located close together on one chromosome
present on the Y chromosome only

blocks.explanation: Modern re-statement: 'genes that are located on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis' (18.2).

book_ref.quote: genes that are located on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis

blocks.prompt: 25 Independent assortment happens because during meiosis:

options.text: homologous chromosome pairs line up randomly
genes move from one chromosome to another

blocks.explanation: Homologous pairs line up randomly in meiosis, giving different combinations of maternal and paternal alleles in gametes (18.2).

book_ref.quote: homologous chromosome pairs line up randomly during meiosis

blocks.prompt: 26 In humans, the random alignment of 23 chromosome pairs can produce allele combinations in one gamete numbering over:
blocks.explanation: In humans independent assortment can produce over 8 million (2²³) possible allele combinations in one gamete (18.2).

book_ref.quote: In humans, it can produce over 8 million

blocks.text: 18.2.1 Limitations to the Law of Independent Assortment

blocks.prompt: 27 Genes close together on the same chromosome are often inherited together, not independently. This is called:
blocks.explanation: Linked genes close together on one chromosome are inherited together; this phenomenon is gene linkage (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: Genes close together on the same chromosome are often inherited together

blocks.prompt: 28 The phenomenon in which one gene controls multiple characters is:
blocks.explanation: Pleiotropy: one gene controls multiple characters, which can distort the expected ratios of independent assortment (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: It is the phenomenon where one gene controls multiple characters

blocks.prompt: 29 Chromosome crossover, a limitation to independent assortment, is the exchange of genetic material between:

options.text: X and Y chromosomes at fertilization

blocks.explanation: Chromosome crossover is the exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes during meiosis (18.2.1).

book_ref.quote: It is the exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes during meiosis

blocks.prompt: 30 For a cross like AaBbCcDdEe × AaBbCcDdEe, outcomes are worked out with probability rules because:

options.text: probability works only for many genes

blocks.explanation: Punnett squares are used for one or two genes; for many genes they become too complex, so probability rules are used (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: So, probability rules are used instead

blocks.prompt: 31 Green pea seeds appear 600 times out of 2,400 seeds. The probability of a green seed is:
blocks.explanation: Probability = number of times the event occurs ÷ total outcomes = 600 ÷ 2,400 = 0.25, i.e. 1 in 4 (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Probability is calculated by dividing the number of times an event occurs

blocks.prompt: 32 The chance of two or more independent events happening together is found by:

options.text: subtracting the smaller probability from the larger
dividing one probability by the other

blocks.explanation: Product rule: the chance of independent events happening together = product of their individual probabilities (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: the chance of two or more independent events happening together is calculated by multiplying

blocks.prompt: 33 In the cross RrYy × RrYy, the probability of a wrinkled green (rryy) offspring is:
blocks.explanation: P(wrinkled) = 1/4 and P(green) = 1/4; by the product rule P(rryy) = (1/4) × (1/4) = 1/16 (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Probability of Round seed = 3/4, Probability of yellow seed = 3/4

blocks.prompt: 34 In the cross RrYy × RrYy, the probability of a round green offspring is:
blocks.explanation: P(round) = 3/4 and P(green) = 1/4, so P(round green) = (3/4) × (1/4) = 3/16 (product rule, 18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: The product rule can be used to predict fertilization outcomes

blocks.prompt: 35 Three dice are rolled together. The chance of getting three sixes is:
blocks.explanation: Each die gives a six with probability 1/6; for three independent dice, (1/6) × (1/6) × (1/6) = 1/216 (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: For two dice, the chance of getting two sixes is

blocks.prompt: 36 In the cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc (genes assorting independently), the probability of an aabbcc offspring is:
blocks.explanation: For each gene P(recessive homozygote) = (1/2) × (1/2) = 1/4; for three genes (1/4) × (1/4) × (1/4) = 1/64 (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: Each parent has a 1/2 chance of giving gamete with allele a

blocks.prompt: 37 The sum rule of probability applies to events that are:

options.text: mutually exclusive (only one can happen at a time)

blocks.explanation: The sum rule applies to mutually exclusive events; the probability of either event is the sum of their probabilities (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: This rule applies to mutually exclusive events

blocks.prompt: 38 In the cross Aa × Aa, the probability of a heterozygous (Aa) offspring, worked out with the sum rule, is:
blocks.explanation: Aa arises two ways (A from male + a from female, a from male + A from female), each 1/4: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 (18.2.2).

book_ref.quote: In a cross Aa × Aa, dominant phenotype (AA or Aa) can occur in three ways

blocks.prompt: 39 In a Yy pea plant, Y is fully expressed and y is not expressed at all. This is:
blocks.explanation: When the dominant allele is fully expressed and the recessive not at all, it is complete dominance (18.3).

book_ref.quote: This is called complete dominance

blocks.prompt: 40 When a heterozygous individual shows a phenotype intermediate between those of both parents, the inheritance is:
blocks.explanation: In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant, so the heterozygote is intermediate, e.g. pink four-o'clock flowers (18.3.1).

book_ref.quote: the heterozygous individual shows a phenotype that is intermediate between phenotypes of both parents

blocks.prompt: 41 In Japanese four-o'clock plants, a cross of red (RR) × white (WW) gives F1 offspring that are:
blocks.explanation: Red × white gives all heterozygous pink (RW) offspring, showing neither R nor W is completely dominant (18.3.1).

book_ref.quote: it produces all heterozygous pink flowered (RW) offspring

blocks.prompt: 42 In four-o'clock plants, a cross between two pink plants gives red, pink and white offspring in the ratio:
blocks.explanation: RW × RW gives red (RR), pink (RW) and white (WW) in a 1:2:1 ratio; genotype and phenotype ratios are the same (18.3.1).

book_ref.quote: When two pink flowered plants (RW × RW) are crossed

blocks.prompt: 43 The type of inheritance in which both alleles of a gene pair are fully expressed in a heterozygote, without blending, is:
blocks.explanation: In co-dominance both alleles work without blending or masking, so both products appear in the heterozygote (18.3.2).

book_ref.quote: both alleles in a gene pair are fully expressed in a heterozygous individual

blocks.prompt: 44 In the MN blood group alleles Lᴹ and Lᴺ, the letter 'L' stands for:
blocks.explanation: 'L' stands for Landsteiner and Levine, who discovered the MN system in 1927 (18.3.2).

book_ref.quote: the scientists who discovered this system in 1927

blocks.prompt: 45 The MN system is also called the MNS system because:

options.text: it has three co-dominant alleles M, N and S
the genes of MN and S/s groups are linked on the same chromosome
S is the antigen of AB people

blocks.explanation: It is called MNS because the genes of the MN group and the S/s group are physically linked on the same chromosome (18.3.2).

book_ref.quote: It is also called the MNS system because the genes of MN group

blocks.prompt: 46 A person with genotype LᴹLᴺ has blood group:
blocks.explanation: Lᴹ and Lᴺ are co-dominant, so LᴹLᴺ carries both M and N antigens: blood group MN (18.3.2).

book_ref.quote: individuals with both M and N antigens

blocks.prompt: 47 In which pattern do the two genes of a heterozygote blend their phenotypic effects?
blocks.explanation: In incomplete dominance the genes blend their effects; in co-dominance both are fully expressed (comparison table, 18.3.2).

book_ref.quote: In heterozygous state, both genes blend their phenotypic effects

blocks.prompt: 48 Which pair are both examples of co-dominance?

options.text: Human MN blood group and human AB blood group
Four-o'clock flower colour and AB blood group
Wheat grain colour and MN blood group
Labrador coat colour and Rh blood group

blocks.explanation: The comparison table gives human MN and AB blood groups as examples of co-dominance; four-o'clock colour is incomplete dominance (18.3.2).

book_ref.quote: Example: Human MN blood group and human AB blood group

blocks.prompt: 49 A multiple allelic system occurs when, in a population, a gene has:
blocks.explanation: A multiple allelic system: a gene has more than two alternative forms (alleles) in a population, creating more variation (18.3.3).

book_ref.quote: occurs when a gene has more than two alternative forms (alleles) in a population

blocks.prompt: 50 Out of the three alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i, the number of alleles carried by one person is:
blocks.explanation: The I gene has three alleles in the population, but each person has only two of them (18.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Each person has only two of these alleles

blocks.prompt: 51 The three alleles of the I gene, in different combinations, produce how many ABO blood groups?
blocks.explanation: Combinations of Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i produce four blood groups: A, B, AB and O (18.3.3).

book_ref.quote: Different combinations produce four blood groups

blocks.prompt: 52 The International Society of Blood Transfusion recognizes how many blood group systems in humans?
blocks.explanation: The International Society of Blood Transfusion recognizes 43 blood group systems in humans (18.4).

book_ref.quote: recognizes 43 blood group systems in humans

blocks.prompt: 53 In blood group systems, the antigens on the surface of RBCs may be:
blocks.explanation: The antigens on RBC surfaces may be proteins, carbohydrates, glycoproteins or glycolipids (18.4).

book_ref.quote: the antigens present on the surface of RBCs may be proteins

blocks.prompt: 54 For blood transfusion, the donor's and recipient's blood must be matched for:
blocks.explanation: The ABO system is the most important and Rh the second; both must be matched for transfusion (18.4).

book_ref.quote: the matching of ABO and Rh-system is necessary

blocks.prompt: 55 The antigens Luᵃ and Luᵇ belong to which blood group system?
blocks.explanation: In the table of other major systems, Lutheran has Luᵃ and Luᵇ; such systems usually do not cause transfusion matching problems (18.4).

book_ref.quote: these usually do not cause matching problems in the blood transfusions

blocks.prompt: 56 Antigens K, k, Kpᵃ, Kpᵇ, Jsᵃ and Jsᵇ belong to the:
blocks.explanation: The table lists K, k, Kpᵃ, Kpᵇ, Jsᵃ and Jsᵇ as the well-known antigens of the Kell system (18.4).

book_ref.quote: The following are the other major blood group system

blocks.prompt: 57 The ABO blood group system was discovered by Landsteiner in:
blocks.explanation: Landsteiner discovered the ABO system in 1901, finding antigen-A and antigen-B on RBCs (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The ABO system was discovered by Landsteiner in 1901

blocks.prompt: 58 People who secrete antigens A and B in saliva, tears and urine possess a dominant secretor gene 'Se' on chromosome:
blocks.explanation: Secretors possess a dominant secretor gene 'Se' on chromosome 19 (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: They possess a dominant secretor gene

blocks.prompt: 59 The rule that a person's plasma contains antibodies against the ABO antigen s/he does not have is called:
blocks.explanation: Plasma has antibodies against the antigen the person lacks (A → anti-B, B → anti-A): Landsteiner's rule of antigen-antibody relationship (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: This is called Landsteiner

blocks.prompt: 60 The gene I, which controls the ABO system, is located on chromosome:
blocks.explanation: The gene I ('iso-haem-agglutinogen') is located on chromosome 9 and has multiple alleles Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: It is located on chromosome 9 and has multiple alleles

blocks.prompt: 61 In the ABO system, allele i:
blocks.explanation: Iᴬ produces antigen-A, Iᴮ produces antigen-B and allele i does not produce any antigen; i is recessive to both (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: Allele i does not produce any antigen

blocks.prompt: 62 The plasma of a person with genotype ii contains:
blocks.explanation: Genotype ii makes neither antigen (blood group O), so its plasma contains both anti-A and anti-B antibodies (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: produces neither antigen-A nor antigen-B

blocks.prompt: 63 A man of genotype Iᴬi marries a woman of genotype ii. The probability that their child has blood group O is:
blocks.explanation: Iᴬi × ii gives Iᴬi (A) and ii (O) in equal numbers, since i is recessive: P(O) = 1/2 (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: The alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ are co-dominant over each other

blocks.prompt: 64 In a transfusion between incompatible blood groups, the recipient's antibodies attack donor RBC antigens and cause:
blocks.explanation: The recipient's antibodies attack the antigens on the donor's RBCs, causing clumping (agglutination) of RBCs (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: It causing clumping (agglutination) of RBCs

blocks.prompt: 65 A person of blood group B will show agglutination if given blood of group:
blocks.explanation: Agglutination occurs if group A receives group B and vice versa (and if AB blood is given to A, B or O) (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: If blood group A individual receives blood group B and vice versa

blocks.prompt: 66 Two parents who both have blood group O (ii) can have children of blood group:
blocks.explanation: ii × ii gives all ii offspring (blood group O); this is one reason the allele i is frequent in the population (18.4.1).

book_ref.quote: In a cross between blood group O (ii) and O (ii), all offspring

blocks.prompt: 67 The name of the Rh blood group system is derived from:

options.text: the Rhesus monkey, in which its antigen was first discovered

blocks.explanation: Rh comes from the Rhesus monkey, in which Landsteiner first discovered its antigen in the 1930s (18.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The name of this system (Rh) is derived from Rhesus monkey

blocks.prompt: 68 The Rh-antigen on RBCs is also called:
blocks.explanation: The Rh system is based on the presence or absence of Rh-antigen, also called Rh factor or antigen-D (18.4.2).

book_ref.quote: also called Rh factor or antigen-D

blocks.prompt: 69 A person who has antigen-A on the RBCs but lacks the Rh-antigen has blood group:
blocks.explanation: Blood groups name both systems together: antigen-A without Rh-antigen is A-negative (18.4.2).

book_ref.quote: The individual who has antigen-A but lack Rh-antigen will have blood group A-negative

blocks.prompt: 70 A person with genotype Dd is:
blocks.explanation: The dominant allele D forms the Rh-antigen, so DD and Dd are Rh-positive; only dd is Rh-negative (18.4.2).

book_ref.quote: individuals with genotypes DD or Dd have Rh-antigen and are Rh-positive

blocks.prompt: 71 Unlike the ABO system, in the Rh system anti-Rh antibodies:

options.text: are made only after an Rh-negative person is exposed to Rh-positive blood
are naturally present in every Rh-negative person

blocks.explanation: Rh-negative people do not naturally have anti-Rh antibodies; they form them after receiving Rh-positive blood (18.4.2).

book_ref.quote: Rh-negative people do not naturally have anti-Rh antibodies

blocks.prompt: 72 Once an Rh-negative person has formed anti-Rh antibodies, these antibodies:

options.text: are passed to all his sons
stay in the body for life

blocks.explanation: Anti-Rh antibodies formed after receiving Rh-positive blood destroy the donated RBCs and stay in the body for life (18.4.2).

book_ref.quote: These antibodies stay in the body for life

blocks.prompt: 73 Erythroblastosis foetalis is a haemolytic disease caused by:

options.text: Rh incompatibility between an Rh-positive mother and an Rh-negative foetus
Rh incompatibility between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive foetus

blocks.explanation: It is a haemolytic disease of the foetus/new-born caused by Rh incompatibility between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive foetus (18.4.3).

book_ref.quote: caused by Rh incompatibility between Rh-negative pregnant mother and Rh-positive foetus

blocks.prompt: 74 In erythroblastosis foetalis, the substance produced by breakdown of foetal RBCs that builds up and can damage brain cells is:
blocks.explanation: Breakdown of RBCs produces bilirubin, which builds up, causes jaundice and at high levels can damage brain cells (18.4.3).

book_ref.quote: The breakdown of RBCs produces bilirubin

blocks.prompt: 75 In a surviving foetus with erythroblastosis foetalis, the liver and spleen become enlarged because they:
blocks.explanation: If the foetus survives, the liver and spleen enlarge as they try to make more RBCs (18.4.3).

book_ref.quote: the liver and spleen become enlarged because they try to make more RBCs

blocks.prompt: 76 To prevent Rh sensitization, the mother is injected during early pregnancy and immediately after birth with:
blocks.explanation: Rh-antiserum destroys any baby's RBCs that crossed into the mother's blood before her immune system is sensitized (18.4.3).

book_ref.quote: serum containing anti-Rh antibodies

blocks.prompt: 77 An O-negative mother carrying an A-positive baby is often protected from forming anti-Rh antibodies because:

options.text: her anti-A antibodies quickly destroy foetal RBCs entering her blood

blocks.explanation: ABO incompatibility can protect: her already present anti-A or anti-B antibodies destroy entering foetal RBCs before anti-Rh forms (18.4.3).

book_ref.quote: Sometimes ABO incompatibility protects the baby against Rh incompatibility

blocks.prompt: 78 Polygenic traits typically show:
blocks.explanation: Polygenic traits show a range of differences, i.e. continuous variation, e.g. height, skin colour, weight (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Polygenic traits show a range of differences

blocks.prompt: 79 In polygenic inheritance, the alleles of many genes contribute to the same trait:

options.text: by one allele masking all the others

blocks.explanation: All alleles of many genes contribute to the same trait in an additive way; their combined effect produces a single trait (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: all alleles of many genes contribute to the same trait in an additive way

blocks.prompt: 80 Human skin colour, which depends on the amount of melanin, is controlled by about:
blocks.explanation: Skin colour is controlled by polygenes (about 60 genes); for understanding, three genes A, B, C are taken (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: This trait is controlled by polygenes (about 60 genes)

blocks.prompt: 81 In the three-gene model of skin colour, what fraction of children of two AaBbCc parents is expected to have the intermediate (middle) colour?
blocks.explanation: The ratio 1:6:15:20:15:6:1 adds to 64; the middle class (three dark alleles) is 20/64 (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: The ratio of different skin colours will be 1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1

blocks.prompt: 82 Parents with genotypes AABBCC (very dark) and aabbcc (very light) will have children who are:

options.text: very dark and very light in 1:1

blocks.explanation: AABBCC × aabbcc gives all AaBbCc children of intermediate colour (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: all of their children will be AaBbCc (intermediate colour)

blocks.prompt: 83 In the F2 of dark red (AABBCC) × white (aabbcc) wheat, out of 64 plants, how many show shades of red between the two extremes?
blocks.explanation: Only one F2 plant has darkest red grains (AABBCC) and one has white grains; 62 show shades from moderate to very light red (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: While 62 plants will show different shades of red

blocks.prompt: 84 Besides the three polygenes, wheat grain colour is also influenced by:
blocks.explanation: Environmental factors like light, water and nutrients also influence wheat grain colour (18.5.1).

book_ref.quote: Environmental factors like light, water and nutrients also influence the grain colour

blocks.prompt: 85 Which of the following is an allelic interaction?
blocks.explanation: Allelic interactions (same gene) include incomplete dominance, co-dominance and multiple alleles; epistasis is non-allelic (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: In allelic interactions, alleles of the same gene interact with each other

blocks.prompt: 86 In epistasis, the allele whose effect is masked or modified by an allele of another gene is called:
blocks.explanation: The allele that masks is epistatic; the allele whose effect is masked or modified is hypostatic (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: the allele whose effect is masked or modified is called hypostatic

blocks.prompt: 87 Unlike polygenic inheritance, epistasis usually produces:
blocks.explanation: Polygenic genes each add a small effect (continuous variation); in epistasis one allele masks another, usually giving discontinuous variation (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: This usually produces discontinuous variation

blocks.prompt: 88 In humans, the allele of baldness is epistatic to the alleles of:
blocks.explanation: The book's human example: the allele of baldness is epistatic to the alleles of black and blonde hair (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: the allele of baldness is epistatic to the alleles of black and blonde hair

blocks.prompt: 89 A Labrador dog of genotype BBee has a coat colour that is:
blocks.explanation: Recessive e is epistatic to B and b and blocks pigment deposition in fur, so any ee dog is yellow (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: but ee will have yellow coat

blocks.prompt: 90 Two heterozygous black Labradors (BbEe × BbEe) produce black, brown and yellow puppies in the ratio:
blocks.explanation: BbEe × BbEe gives 9 black : 3 brown : 4 yellow (all ee are yellow) (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: the offspring show black, brown, and yellow colours in a 9:3:4 ratio

blocks.prompt: 91 A Labrador of genotype bbEe has a coat that is:
blocks.explanation: bb gives brown pigment, and E allows its deposition in the fur, so bbEe is brown (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: The B gene controls pigment colour

blocks.prompt: 92 A person with alleles Iᴬ and Iᴮ but genotype hh shows blood group O because no H substance is made. This is called:
blocks.explanation: Without H substance, Iᴬ and Iᴮ cannot make A and B antigens; this O phenotype is the Bombay phenotype, discovered in Bombay in 1952 (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: This phenotype is called Bombay phenotype because it was discovered in Bombay in 1952

blocks.prompt: 93 A foxglove plant DdWw is self-fertilized. White, dark red and light red flowers appear in the ratio:
blocks.explanation: Every plant with at least one W is white (12/16); D_ww is dark red (3/16) and ddww light red (1/16) (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: it produces plants with white, dark red and light red flowers in 12:3:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 94 A foxglove plant of genotype ddww has flowers that are:
blocks.explanation: dd makes light red pigment and ww allows its uniform distribution, so ddww is light red (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: The recessive w allows uniform pigment distribution

blocks.prompt: 95 In foxglove, the dominant allele W:

options.text: limits the pigment to small spots so petals appear white from outside

blocks.explanation: W (at another locus) limits pigment made by D and d to small spots, so petals appear white from outside (18.5.2).

book_ref.quote: limits the distribution of pigment (produced by D and d) in the form of small spots

blocks.prompt: 96 Humans have about how many genes on 23 chromosomes (present in two sets)?
blocks.explanation: Humans have about 20,000 genes on 23 chromosomes; Drosophila about 13,000 genes on 4 chromosomes (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: humans have about 20,000 genes on 23 chromosome

blocks.prompt: 97 Which genes assort independently during gamete formation?

options.text: Closely linked genes on one chromosome
Only genes on the Y chromosome
Genes on different chromosomes or far apart on the same chromosome

blocks.explanation: Closely linked genes stay together; genes on different chromosomes or far apart on one chromosome assort independently (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: or those far apart on the same chromosome, assort independently

blocks.prompt: 98 In a cross for detecting linkage, parental and new phenotypes appear in an equal 1:1:1:1 ratio. This shows the genes are:
blocks.explanation: Equal 1:1:1:1 parental and new phenotypes means the genes are not linked and assort independently (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: If offspring show parental and new phenotypes in equal 1:1:1:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 99 If only parental combinations appear and no new combinations are seen, it shows:
blocks.explanation: Only parental combinations means complete linkage: the genes are very close and do not separate (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: it shows complete linkage, meaning the genes are very close

blocks.prompt: 100 Parental combinations are more frequent and new combinations fewer. This indicates:

options.text: incomplete linkage, with separation by crossing over

blocks.explanation: More parental and fewer new combinations indicate incomplete linkage: linked genes that can separate by crossing over (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: it indicates incomplete linkage, meaning genes are linked but can separate due to crossing over

blocks.prompt: 101 Gene linkage can be observed only when a cross:

options.text: produces a large number of offspring

blocks.explanation: Linkage can only be observed with a large progeny; the larger the progeny, the more it represents the actual frequency (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: Gene linkage can only be observed when a cross produces large number of offspring

blocks.prompt: 102 In Morgan's cross of F1 Drosophila (long wings, broad abdomen), the F2 he actually observed was:

options.text: 3/4 long wings-broad abdomen and 1/4 vestigial wings-narrow abdomen

blocks.explanation: Instead of 9:3:3:1, only parental combinations appeared: 3/4 long-broad and 1/4 vestigial-narrow, so the genes are on the same chromosome (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: There were 3/4 flies with long wings-broad abdomen

blocks.prompt: 103 In Morgan's linkage study of Drosophila, the dominant alleles were:
blocks.explanation: Long wings (L) is dominant over vestigial (l), and broad abdomen (B) is dominant over narrow abdomen (b) (18.6.1).

book_ref.quote: allele for broad abdomen (B) is dominant over narrow abdomen (b)

blocks.prompt: 104 Crossing over, responsible for recombination of linked genes, takes place during:
blocks.explanation: During gamete formation (meiosis-I) homologous chromosomes go through crossing over (18.6.2).

book_ref.quote: During the formation of gametes (meiosis-I), homologous chromosomes go through crossing over

blocks.prompt: 105 During crossing over, the chromatids of two homologous chromosomes swap sections of DNA as the DNA strands:
blocks.explanation: Chromatids line up and swap sections of DNA; DNA strands actually break and re-join (18.6.2).

book_ref.quote: DNA strands actually break and re-join

blocks.prompt: 106 After crossing over, the chromatids involved:

options.text: become identical to the sister chromatids
have the same genes in the same order, but rearranged alleles

blocks.explanation: Recombinant chromatids keep the same genes in the same order, but the alleles are rearranged, giving variety in gametes (18.6.2).

book_ref.quote: still have the same genes in the same order

blocks.prompt: 107 The karyotype of an organism includes:

options.text: the sequence of all its genes
the numbers, sizes and shapes of chromosomes

blocks.explanation: Karyotype is the appearance of the complete set of chromosomes: their numbers, sizes and shapes (18.7).

book_ref.quote: Karyotype includes the numbers, sizes, and shapes of chromosomes

blocks.prompt: 108 Chromosomes that are perfectly similar in the female and the male are called:
blocks.explanation: Chromosomes perfectly similar in both sexes are autosomes; the one differing pair are the sex chromosomes (18.7).

book_ref.quote: The chromosomes which are perfectly similar in female and male, are called autosomes

blocks.prompt: 109 In Drosophila and mammals, the Y chromosome is described as:
blocks.explanation: The sex chromosome pair has a rod-shaped X chromosome and a hook-shaped Y chromosome (18.7).

book_ref.quote: a rod-shaped X chromosome and a hook-shaped Y chromosome

blocks.prompt: 110 Drosophila has:

options.text: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes
11 pairs of autosomes and an XO pair
4 pairs of autosomes and no sex chromosomes
3 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes

blocks.explanation: Drosophila has 3 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes; humans have 22 pairs and 1 pair (18.7).

book_ref.quote: Drosophila has 3 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes

blocks.prompt: 111 In the XX-XY system, females are called homogametic because they:

options.text: produce all eggs with one X chromosome

blocks.explanation: Females produce all eggs with one X chromosome (homogametic); males produce X and Y sperms (heterogametic) (18.7).

book_ref.quote: females are homogametic which means that they produce all eggs with one X chromosome

blocks.prompt: 112 A male grasshopper has a total of how many chromosomes?
blocks.explanation: The grasshopper has 22 autosomes; the male is XO, so it has 23 chromosomes, the female (XX) has 24 (18.7).

book_ref.quote: Male has total 23 chromosomes because its sex chromosome pair is XO

blocks.prompt: 113 In the XX-XO system, a gamete without any sex chromosome is called:
blocks.explanation: The XO male forms half sperms with X and half without any sex chromosome; the latter are nullo gametes (18.7).

book_ref.quote: A gamete without any sex chromosome is called nullo gamete

blocks.prompt: 114 In birds (ZW-ZZ system), the heterogametic sex is the:
blocks.explanation: In birds females are ZW and produce Z and W eggs; males are ZZ and all sperms carry Z (18.7).

book_ref.quote: the sex chromosomes are ZW in females and ZZ in males

blocks.prompt: 115 In birds, a Z-carrying egg fertilized by a sperm gives:
blocks.explanation: Every sperm carries Z: a Z egg gives a ZZ male, and a W-carrying egg gives a ZW female (18.7).

book_ref.quote: When an Z carrying egg is fertilized by the sperm, offspring is male

blocks.prompt: 116 Traits whose alleles are found on both X and Y chromosomes, and which are equally distributed in males and females, are called:
blocks.explanation: Alleles of very few traits are on both X and Y; these are X-Y-linked or pseudo-autosomal traits (18.8).

book_ref.quote: are called X-Y-linked or pseudo-autosomal traits

blocks.prompt: 117 A sex-linked trait is actually X-linked because:

options.text: the Y chromosome usually carries almost no functional genes
the X chromosome is smaller than Y
the Y chromosome carries all the alleles

blocks.explanation: Sex-linked traits are actually X-linked because the Y chromosome usually carries almost no functional genes (18.8).

book_ref.quote: usually the Y chromosome carries almost no functional genes

blocks.prompt: 118 In 1910, the mutant male Drosophila that Morgan observed had:

options.text: white eyes instead of normal red

blocks.explanation: In 1910 Morgan observed a mutant male Drosophila with white eyes instead of normal red (18.8).

book_ref.quote: In 1910, Thomas Hunt Morgan observed a male Drosophila fly

blocks.prompt: 119 The important observation in Morgan's F2 (red-eyed F1 × red-eyed F1) was that:

options.text: all the white-eyed flies were females
white and red appeared 1:1 in both sexes
all the white-eyed flies were males

blocks.explanation: Out of 4252 F2 flies, 782 (about 18%) were white-eyed, and all of them were males (18.8).

book_ref.quote: All of the white-eyed F2 flies were males

blocks.prompt: 120 When Morgan mated a white-eyed female with a red-eyed male, the offspring were:

options.text: all females red-eyed and all males white-eyed
all females white-eyed and all males red-eyed

blocks.explanation: White-eyed female × red-eyed male gave all red-eyed females and all white-eyed males, showing the gene is on the X chromosome (18.8).

book_ref.quote: All female offspring had red eyes, and all male offspring had white eyes

blocks.prompt: 121 Morgan test-crossed the F1 red-eyed female with a white-eyed male. He obtained red- and white-eyed males and females in the ratio:
blocks.explanation: The testcross gave white- and red-eyed males and females in 1:1:1:1, proving a female could have white eyes (18.8).

book_ref.quote: He obtained both white-eyed and red-eyed males and females in a 1:1:1:1 ratio

blocks.prompt: 122 Amniocentesis, a method of embryonic screening, is generally done during:
blocks.explanation: Amniocentesis is generally done between the 15th and 20th week; foetal cells from amniotic fluid are cultured and checked for chromosome number (18.8).

book_ref.quote: Amniocentesis is generally done during 15th and 20th week of pregnancy

blocks.prompt: 123 A woman is a carrier (heterozygous) of an X-linked recessive trait. The proportion of her sons that can inherit the trait is:
blocks.explanation: A carrier mother passes the recessive X to half her sons; a son needs only one allele to show the trait (18.8.1).

book_ref.quote: If mother is a carrier (heterozygous) of the trait, 50% of her sons can inherit it

blocks.prompt: 124 A man has an X-linked recessive trait and his wife is normal (not a carrier). Their children will be:

options.text: all daughters carriers and no son affected

blocks.explanation: Daughters get their father's X, so all are carriers; sons get his Y, so no son inherits the trait (18.8.1).

blocks.prompt: 125 Which of the following is an X-linked dominant trait?
blocks.explanation: X-linked dominant examples: vitamin D-resistant rickets, Rett syndrome, Aicardi syndrome (18.8.1).

book_ref.quote: Examples include vitamin D-resistant rickets

blocks.prompt: 126 A father shows an X-linked dominant trait. Which of his children inherit it?

options.text: All his sons and none of his daughters
Half his sons and half his daughters
All his daughters and none of his sons

blocks.explanation: A daughter inherits her father's X chromosome and a son does not, so all daughters and no sons inherit it (18.8.1).

book_ref.quote: all of his daughters will inherit it

blocks.prompt: 127 Y-linked genes that have no alleles on the X chromosome are called:
blocks.explanation: Y-linked genes without alleles on X are holandric (hemizygous) genes, on the non-homologous region of Y (18.8.1).

blocks.prompt: 128 Growth of hair on the rim of the pinna (hypertrichosis) is an example of:

blocks.prompt: 129 Haemophilia B is due to an abnormal blood clotting factor:
blocks.explanation: Haemophilia A: factor VIII; haemophilia B: factor IX (both X-linked recessive); haemophilia C: factor XI (18.8.2).

book_ref.quote: Haemophilia A and B are due to abnormal blood clotting factors VIII and IX, respectively

blocks.prompt: 130 Haemophilia C occurs in both genders equally because it is:

blocks.prompt: 131 The SRY gene on the human Y chromosome produces a protein that:

options.text: starts development of testes and prevents female reproductive structures

blocks.prompt: 132 In the clotting cascade, the soluble protein fibrinogen is converted into:

blocks.prompt: 133 Abnormal clotting due to disruption of the balance of the clotting system is known as:

blocks.prompt: 134 The gene for the blue opsin is located on:

blocks.prompt: 135 Green blindness in dichromacy is called:
blocks.explanation: Dichromacy may be red-blindness (protanopia), green blindness (deuteranopia) or blue-blindness (tritanopia) (18.8.2).

book_ref.quote: It may be red-blindness (protanopia), green blindness (deuteranopia)

blocks.prompt: 136 The specific pigment proteins of the cone cells of the retina are called:
blocks.explanation: Each of the red-, green- and blue-sensitive cones contains its specific pigment proteins called opsins (18.8.2).

blocks.prompt: 137 The most common of the more than 30 muscular dystrophies is:

book_ref.quote: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is the most common

blocks.prompt: 138 A male who receives the recessive allele of Duchenne muscular dystrophy cannot make the muscle protein:

blocks.prompt: 139 In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, most patients are unable to walk and need a wheelchair by about the age of:

blocks.prompt: 140 In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, about two thirds of cases are inherited from the mother, while about one third are due to:

blocks.prompt: 141 In managing muscular dystrophy, corticosteroid medicines are used to:

blocks.prompt: 142 Sex-limited and sex-influenced traits are NOT sex-linked because:

options.text: their alleles are on the Y chromosome
their alleles are not present on sex chromosomes

book_ref.quote: because their alleles are not present on sex chromosomes

blocks.prompt: 143 Both male and female sheep have the genes for horn development, but horns develop only in males. This is a:

blocks.prompt: 144 Phenotypic difference between males and females of the same species (sexual dimorphism) is due to:
blocks.explanation: Sex-limited genes are responsible for sexual dimorphism (18.8.3).

book_ref.quote: Sex-limited genes are responsible for sexual dimorphism

blocks.prompt: 145 Baldness is a sex-influenced trait. A man of genotype Bb (B = baldness allele) is:

bald, because the baldness allele is dominant in men
bald only if he is old

blocks.prompt: 146 In sex-influenced traits, the same allele is dominant in one sex and recessive in the other because of:

hormonal difference between males and females
